safe_alternatives: 1. Enjoy fish and dairy items together or separately based on culinary preference.\n2. Protect depigmented skin zones from ultraviolet radiation using SPF 50+ sunscreens.\n3. Consult clinical dermatologists for targeted light therapies or topical treatments.
verified_sources: British Association of Dermatologists, National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: sweating out fever thick blankets blankets heat
viral_myth: Wrap yourself in thick blankets to sweat out a fever and break it quickly.
scientific_fact: Trimming yourself in heavy layers traps body heat, dangerously driving internal core temperatures to organ-damaging levels.
possibilities: 1. Thermal Mechanics: Heavy insulation prevents the skin surface from radiating excess heat away.\n2. Dehydration Acceleration: Forces extreme sweating without cooling the body, draining essential fluids.\n3. Hypothalamus Control: The brain's internal thermostat controls fevers, not external sweat levels.
safe_alternatives: 1. Wear single layers of loose, breathable cotton clothing during fever spikes.\n2. Administer antipyretics like paracetamol or ibuprofen to lower the brain's temperature set-point.\n3. Use lukewarm sponge baths if core temperatures remain uncomfortably elevated.
verified_sources: American Academy of Pediatrics, Mayo Clinic

claim_keywords: vape e cigarettes completely harmless water vapor
viral_myth: Vaping and electronic cigarettes are completely harmless because they only emit water vapor.
scientific_fact: Vape aerosols contain highly addictive nicotine, toxic heavy metals, and volatile organic compounds that cause severe lung injury.
possibilities: 1. Chemical Delivery: Emits ultra-fine chemical particles, formaldehydes, and oils, not pure water vapor.\n2. Lung Pathology: Inhaling heated solvents triggers widespread broncho-alveolar tissue inflammation.\n3. Addiction Pathway: Delivers highly concentrated nicotine, altering adolescent neuro-development.
safe_alternatives: 1. Access evidence-based smoking and vaping cessation support programs.\n2. Utilize FDA-approved nicotine replacement therapies (patches, gums) if quitting.\n3. Maintain clean, chemical-free airways to preserve long-term respiratory metrics.
verified_sources: US Surgeon General, World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: bold coffee burns fat caffeine weight loss
viral_myth: Drinking bulletproof coffee with butter burns fat instantly without exercise.
scientific_fact: Adding heavy fats like butter or coconut oil to coffee loads it with pure saturated calories, promoting weight gain if not accounted for.
possibilities: 1. Caloric Density: Adding fats injects 200–400 extra calories into your morning drink.\n2. Caffeine Mechanics: Caffeine slightly increases temporary metabolic rates but cannot override caloric surpluses.\n3. Lipid Elevation: Chronic intake of concentrated saturated fats spikes ApoB and LDL cholesterol levels.
safe_alternatives: 1. Enjoy black coffee or coffee with low-fat milk as a low-calorie metabolic option.\n2. Track total daily caloric balances instead of relying on miraculous beverage configurations.\n3. Focus on whole-food nutrient matrices to establish stable morning energy levels.
verified_sources: American College of Cardiology, India First Video Fact Check

claim_keywords: honey safe diabetes natural sweetener
viral_myth: Honey is natural, so people with diabetes can eat it freely.
scientific_fact: Honey is mostly sugar and raises blood glucose. 'Natural' does not mean it is free of effect on blood sugar.
possibilities: 1. Natural Label: A natural origin does not change how the body processes sugar.\n2. Portion Matters: A small amount counted within a meal plan may be acceptable.\n3. Risk: Large or frequent amounts can push glucose too high.
safe_alternatives: 1. Count honey as part of your daily carbohydrate allowance.\n2. Ask a dietitian how much, if any, fits your plan.\n3. Check blood glucose after meals to see your own response.
verified_sources: American Diabetes Association (ADA), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: jaggery brown sugar diabetes safe
viral_myth: Jaggery and brown sugar are safe for diabetics because they are natural.
scientific_fact: Jaggery and brown sugar are still forms of sugar and raise blood glucose in much the same way as white sugar.
possibilities: 1. Minor Minerals: Jaggery has trace minerals, but not enough to offset its sugar content.\n2. Same Effect: Blood glucose rises after eating it.\n3. Risk: Switching sugars gives false reassurance and can worsen control.
safe_alternatives: 1. Limit all added sugars, including jaggery and brown sugar.\n2. Choose whole grains, pulses and vegetables for carbohydrates.\n3. Discuss sweeteners with your doctor or dietitian.
verified_sources: American Diabetes Association (ADA), ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians

claim_keywords: diabetes avoid all fruit sugar
viral_myth: People with diabetes must avoid all fruit because fruit is full of sugar.
scientific_fact: Whole fruit contains fiber, vitamins and minerals and can be part of a diabetes meal plan in sensible portions. Fruit juice raises glucose faster than whole fruit.
possibilities: 1. Fiber Benefit: Whole fruit digests more slowly than juice.\n2. Portion Matters: Large servings raise blood glucose.\n3. Individual Variation: Responses differ between people.
safe_alternatives: 1. Choose whole fruit over juice.\n2. Keep to portions suggested by your dietitian.\n3. Pair fruit with a meal or protein and check your glucose response.
verified_sources: American Diabetes Association (ADA), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: diabetes contagious spread touch
viral_myth: Diabetes spreads by touching, sharing food or staying near a diabetic person.
scientific_fact: Diabetes is not an infection and cannot be passed from person to person. Type 1 is an autoimmune condition, and type 2 is linked to genes, weight and lifestyle.
possibilities: 1. No Germ Cause: It is not caused by a virus or bacteria.\n2. Family Risk: Genes can raise risk but this is not contagion.\n3. Stigma Harm: The myth isolates patients.
safe_alternatives: 1. Treat people with diabetes normally and share meals freely.\n2. Get your own blood sugar screened if you have risk factors.\n3. Use official health sources to correct this rumor.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), International Diabetes Federation (IDF)

claim_keywords: insulin injection kidney blindness last resort
viral_myth: Insulin injections cause kidney failure and blindness, so you should avoid them.
scientific_fact: Diabetes complications come from long-term high blood sugar, not from insulin. Insulin is essential for type 1 diabetes and helps many people with type 2.
possibilities: 1. Real Cause: Prolonged uncontrolled glucose damages eyes and kidneys.\n2. Delay Risk: Avoiding needed insulin leads to higher glucose and more damage.\n3. Misconception: Needing insulin is not a personal failure.
safe_alternatives: 1. Take insulin exactly as your doctor prescribes.\n2. Ask your care team about injection technique and fear of needles.\n3. Get regular eye and kidney checks.
verified_sources: American Diabetes Association (ADA), International Diabetes Federation (IDF)

claim_keywords: bitter gourd karela juice cure diabetes
viral_myth: Drinking karela (bitter gourd) juice cures diabetes, so medicines can be stopped.
scientific_fact: Some small studies suggest bitter gourd may slightly lower blood sugar, but the evidence is weak and it is not a cure. It must not replace prescribed treatment.
possibilities: 1. Possible Small Effect: Studies are limited and inconsistent.\n2. No Cure: It does not restore insulin production.\n3. Risk: Stopping medicine can cause dangerous blood sugar levels.
safe_alternatives: 1. Eat karela as a normal vegetable if you like it.\n2. Never stop or reduce medicines without your doctor's advice.\n3. Tell your doctor about any herbal products you take.
verified_sources: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), American Diabetes Association (ADA)

claim_keywords: eggs cholesterol heart avoid completely
viral_myth: Eating eggs raises cholesterol so dangerously that everyone should avoid them.
scientific_fact: For most healthy people, moderate egg intake fits a heart-healthy diet because saturated fat affects blood cholesterol more than the cholesterol in food. People with heart disease or diabetes should follow their doctor's advice.
possibilities: 1. Moderate Intake: One egg a day is considered fine for many healthy adults.\n2. Cooking Matters: Frying in butter or ghee adds saturated fat.\n3. Individual Risk: Heart patients may need limits.
safe_alternatives: 1. Prefer boiled or poached eggs over fried.\n2. Fill your plate with vegetables, pulses and whole grains.\n3. Ask your doctor about egg limits if you have high cholesterol or heart disease.
verified_sources: American Heart Association (AHA), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: high blood pressure no symptoms feel fine
viral_myth: If you feel fine, your blood pressure must be normal.
scientific_fact: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms and is often called a silent killer. Only measuring it shows whether it is high.
possibilities: 1. Silent Condition: Many people feel normal for years.\n2. Hidden Damage: It strains the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes.\n3. Detection: Regular checks are the only reliable way to know.
safe_alternatives: 1. Get your blood pressure measured at least once a year.\n2. Use a validated home monitor if advised by your doctor.\n3. Cut down salt, stay active and take prescribed medicine regularly.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), American Heart Association (AHA)

claim_keywords: sendha namak rock salt no sodium pink salt
viral_myth: Rock salt (sendha namak) or pink salt has no sodium, so you can eat it freely.
scientific_fact: All types of salt, including rock salt and pink salt, contain sodium. Too much sodium raises blood pressure. WHO advises adults to consume less than 5 grams of salt a day.
possibilities: 1. Same Sodium Source: Salt is sodium chloride whatever its color.\n2. Trace Minerals: Tiny amounts are not nutritionally significant.\n3. Risk: Using more because it feels healthier raises sodium intake.
safe_alternatives: 1. Keep total salt under about one teaspoon (5 g) a day.\n2. Check labels on packaged foods, pickles and snacks for hidden salt.\n3. Flavor food with herbs, lemon and spices instead.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), American Heart Association (AHA)

claim_keywords: cough CPR heart attack alone
viral_myth: If you feel a heart attack coming on alone, coughing hard and repeatedly will save your life.
scientific_fact: 'Cough CPR' is not recommended for the public. A heart attack needs emergency medical care right away, so call emergency services immediately.
possibilities: 1. Viral Chain Message: The claim spread widely through forwarded messages.\n2. No Public Guidance: Major heart organizations do not endorse it.\n3. Risk: Delay in calling for help costs lives.
safe_alternatives: 1. Call your local emergency number (112 in India) immediately.\n2. Follow the instructions of the emergency operator.\n3. Stay calm, sit down and unlock the door if you can.
verified_sources: American Heart Association (AHA), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: heart attack only elderly young people
viral_myth: Heart attacks only happen to older people.
scientific_fact: Heart attacks can occur at younger ages, especially with smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol or a family history of heart disease.
possibilities: 1. Risk Factors: Lifestyle and medical conditions raise risk at any age.\n2. Warning Signs: Chest pain, breathlessness and sweating need urgent care.\n3. Risk: Ignoring symptoms in young people delays treatment.
safe_alternatives: 1. Get blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol checked regularly.\n2. Avoid tobacco and stay physically active.\n3. Seek emergency care for chest pain at any age.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), American Heart Association (AHA)

claim_keywords: covid vaccine infertility fertility
viral_myth: COVID-19 vaccines cause infertility in men and women.
scientific_fact: There is no evidence that COVID-19 vaccines cause infertility. Studies have found no effect on fertility, and vaccination is recommended for people who are pregnant or planning pregnancy.
possibilities: 1. Origin: The rumor spread from a false social media claim.\n2. Evidence: Large studies show no fertility harm.\n3. Real Risk: COVID-19 infection itself can be dangerous in pregnancy.
safe_alternatives: 1. Talk to your doctor if you are planning pregnancy.\n2. Use official health pages rather than forwarded messages.\n3. Complete recommended vaccine doses.
verified_sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: natural infection better than vaccine skip childhood vaccination
viral_myth: Getting the disease naturally gives better protection than vaccines, so children should skip vaccines.
scientific_fact: Vaccines build protection without the risk of serious illness or death that diseases like measles can cause. Natural infection can leave children with lasting complications.
possibilities: 1. Disease Risk: Infections can cause pneumonia, brain swelling or death.\n2. Safe Route: Vaccines give immunity without those risks.\n3. Community Effect: High coverage protects babies who cannot be vaccinated yet.
safe_alternatives: 1. Follow the national immunization schedule.\n2. Keep the child's vaccination card up to date.\n3. Ask your pediatrician or health worker about any concerns.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: flu shot gives you flu influenza vaccine
viral_myth: The flu vaccine gives you the flu.
scientific_fact: Flu shots contain inactivated virus or viral parts and cannot cause influenza. Mild side effects like a sore arm or low fever can occur.
possibilities: 1. Side Effects: Short-lived soreness or mild fever is the immune system responding.\n2. Timing Coincidence: People may catch another virus around vaccination time.\n3. Protection: Vaccine reduces risk of severe flu.
safe_alternatives: 1. Get an annual flu vaccine if recommended for you.\n2. Rest and drink fluids if you feel mild after-effects.\n3. See a doctor if symptoms are severe.
verified_sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: too many vaccines overload immune system child
viral_myth: Giving many vaccines to a child overloads their immune system.
scientific_fact: Children's immune systems handle thousands of germs every day. The antigens in vaccines are a tiny fraction of that, and the schedule is tested for safety.
possibilities: 1. Daily Exposure: Everyday life exposes babies to far more antigens than vaccines do.\n2. Testing: Combined schedules are studied before approval.\n3. Risk: Delaying vaccines leaves children unprotected.
safe_alternatives: 1. Follow the recommended schedule on time.\n2. Ask your pediatrician about specific concerns.\n3. Use official immunization pages for accurate information.
verified_sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)

claim_keywords: vaccine microchip tracking 5g
viral_myth: Vaccines contain microchips or tracking devices.
scientific_fact: Vaccines do not contain microchips or tracking devices. Their ingredients are listed publicly and a microchip could not fit through a vaccine needle.
possibilities: 1. Rumor Origin: The claim spread through viral posts.\n2. Ingredient Transparency: Regulators publish ingredient lists.\n3. Impact: Fear causes people to skip protection.
safe_alternatives: 1. Read official vaccine ingredient information.\n2. Ask your health worker or doctor if you are unsure.\n3. Avoid sharing unverified forwards.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: antibiotics every diarrhea loose motions
viral_myth: Antibiotics are needed to treat every case of diarrhea.
scientific_fact: Most diarrhea is caused by viruses and does not need antibiotics. The main treatment is oral rehydration solution (ORS), plus zinc for children.
possibilities: 1. Viral Cause: Antibiotics do not work on viruses.\n2. Resistance Risk: Overuse makes antibiotics less effective.\n3. When Needed: A doctor prescribes them for specific infections.
safe_alternatives: 1. Give ORS and keep drinking fluids.\n2. Give zinc to children as advised by a doctor.\n3. See a doctor if there is blood in the stool or signs of dehydration.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF

claim_keywords: diarrhea stop food water stomach rest dehydration
viral_myth: A person with diarrhea should stop eating and drinking to let the stomach rest.
scientific_fact: People with diarrhea should keep drinking fluids and ORS and continue eating, because dehydration is the main danger.
possibilities: 1. Fluid Loss: Diarrhea drains water and salts quickly.\n2. Feeding: Continued feeding helps recovery.\n3. Danger Signs: Very sleepy, unable to drink or sunken eyes need urgent care.
safe_alternatives: 1. Give ORS in small frequent sips.\n2. Continue breastfeeding and normal feeding for children.\n3. Go to a health facility if danger signs appear.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF

claim_keywords: dengue spreads person to person touch sneeze
viral_myth: Dengue spreads by touching or sneezing from an infected person.
scientific_fact: Dengue is spread by the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, not by casual contact, touch or sneezing.
possibilities: 1. Vector Spread: The virus is passed on by mosquito bites.\n2. Casual Contact: Sitting near a patient does not transmit it.\n3. Prevention Focus: Controlling mosquitoes is what works.
safe_alternatives: 1. Remove stagnant water around the home.\n2. Use repellents and screens to avoid bites.\n3. Seek medical care for high fever with severe symptoms.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP)

claim_keywords: tb spread utensils touching sharing plates
viral_myth: Tuberculosis spreads by sharing utensils or touching a TB patient.
scientific_fact: TB spreads through the air when a person with active lung TB coughs or sneezes, not through utensils, touch or sharing food.
possibilities: 1. Airborne Spread: Tiny droplets carry the bacteria.\n2. Treatment Effect: People on effective treatment quickly become less infectious.\n3. Stigma Harm: The myth causes isolation and delayed treatment.
safe_alternatives: 1. Get tested if you have a cough lasting more than two weeks.\n2. Ensure good ventilation at home.\n3. Complete the full course of TB treatment.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP)

claim_keywords: tb hereditary genetic family disease
viral_myth: Tuberculosis is hereditary and runs in families.
scientific_fact: TB is caused by bacteria and is not inherited. Family members may be infected because of close, prolonged contact, and TB is curable with treatment.
possibilities: 1. Infectious Cause: It spreads through air, not genes.\n2. Household Contact: Close contacts should be screened.\n3. Curable: Full treatment cures drug-sensitive TB.
safe_alternatives: 1. Screen household contacts of a TB patient.\n2. Start and complete treatment under supervision.\n3. Use free government TB services.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP)

claim_keywords: tb medicine stop early symptoms gone
viral_myth: You can stop TB medicines once your cough and fever go away.
scientific_fact: Drug-sensitive TB needs treatment for at least six months. Stopping early can cause relapse and drug-resistant TB.
possibilities: 1. Feeling Better: Symptoms improve before the bacteria are gone.\n2. Resistance Danger: Incomplete treatment creates tougher TB.\n3. Support: Free treatment support exists.
safe_alternatives: 1. Take every dose for the full course.\n2. Talk to your health worker about side effects instead of stopping.\n3. Use adherence support such as DOT or digital reminders.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP)

claim_keywords: steam inhalation gargle salt kill coronavirus
viral_myth: Inhaling hot steam or gargling salt water kills the coronavirus in your body.
scientific_fact: Steam or salt-water gargles do not kill the virus inside the body, and very hot steam can cause burns.
possibilities: 1. Comfort Effect: Steam may ease a blocked nose temporarily.\n2. No Antiviral Action: It does not reach or destroy the virus.\n3. Burn Risk: Hot steam can injure the face and airway.
safe_alternatives: 1. Get vaccinated and follow current health guidance.\n2. Rest, drink fluids and take medicines prescribed by a doctor.\n3. Seek care if breathing becomes difficult.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: haldi turmeric milk cure covid cancer
viral_myth: Haldi doodh (turmeric milk) cures or prevents COVID-19 and cancer.
scientific_fact: Turmeric and curcumin show interesting lab results, but there is not enough human evidence that they cure or prevent COVID-19 or cancer.
possibilities: 1. Food Use: Turmeric in cooking is safe for most people.\n2. Evidence Gap: Lab results have not been confirmed in patients.\n3. Risk: Relying on it can delay real treatment.
safe_alternatives: 1. Enjoy turmeric milk as a normal drink if you like it.\n2. Follow vaccination and standard medical treatment.\n3. Tell your doctor about turmeric supplements, which may interact with medicines.
verified_sources: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), National Institutes of Health (NIH)

claim_keywords: chicken egg bird flu coronavirus eating safe
viral_myth: Eating chicken or eggs spreads bird flu and coronavirus.
scientific_fact: Properly cooked poultry and eggs are safe to eat. The risk comes from handling sick or dead birds, not from well-cooked food.
possibilities: 1. Cooking Effect: Heat kills viruses and bacteria in meat and eggs.\n2. Handling Risk: Contact with sick birds is the main risk.\n3. Misinformation Harm: Panic hurts farmers and nutrition.
safe_alternatives: 1. Cook poultry and eggs thoroughly.\n2. Wash hands and surfaces after handling raw meat.\n3. Avoid contact with sick or dead birds and report outbreaks.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: dog bite chilli turmeric oil wound rabies
viral_myth: After a dog bite, applying chilli, turmeric or oil to the wound is enough.
scientific_fact: Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start but preventable. Wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and get anti-rabies vaccine immediately, with immunoglobulin when needed.
possibilities: 1. Wrong Remedy: Home applications do not stop the virus and can irritate the wound.\n2. Time Critical: Treatment must start soon after exposure.\n3. Life-Saving: Post-exposure treatment is highly effective.
safe_alternatives: 1. Wash the wound with soap and running water for 15 minutes.\n2. Go to a hospital right away for anti-rabies treatment.\n3. Vaccinate pet dogs and avoid stray animals.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: snake bite tourniquet cut suck venom herbal
viral_myth: After a snake bite, tie a tight band, cut the wound or suck out the venom.
scientific_fact: Tight tourniquets, cutting and sucking venom do not help and can cause harm. The person should be kept calm and still and taken to a hospital quickly for antivenom.
possibilities: 1. Harmful Methods: They can damage tissue and delay care.\n2. Time Critical: Antivenom works best when given early.\n3. Traditional Healers: Delay in reaching hospital is a leading cause of death.
safe_alternatives: 1. Keep the person calm and the bitten limb still.\n2. Remove rings and tight items near the bite.\n3. Take the person to a hospital with antivenom immediately.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: nosebleed tilt head back pinch nose
viral_myth: To stop a nosebleed, tilt your head back.
scientific_fact: Tilting the head back lets blood run down the throat. Lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes.
possibilities: 1. Swallowed Blood: It can cause nausea or choking.\n2. Correct Method: Pressure on the soft nose stops most bleeds.\n3. When Serious: Bleeding lasting more than 20 minutes needs care.
safe_alternatives: 1. Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose.\n2. Breathe through your mouth and hold for 10 to 15 minutes.\n3. Seek medical help if bleeding does not stop or follows a head injury.
verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), Mayo Clinic

claim_keywords: seizure fit spoon key onion mouth
viral_myth: Put a spoon, key or onion in the mouth of someone having a seizure.
scientific_fact: Never put anything in the mouth of a person having a seizure. It can break teeth or block the airway. Protect the head, turn them on their side and time the seizure.
possibilities: 1. Tongue Myth: People cannot swallow their tongue during a seizure.\n2. Injury Risk: Objects cause choking and dental injury.\n3. Right Response: Safety and positioning matter.
safe_alternatives: 1. Move hard objects away and cushion the head.\n2. Turn the person onto their side once the shaking stops.\n3. Call emergency services if it lasts over 5 minutes or repeats.
verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: stroke prick fingers needle bleed ears
viral_myth: If someone has a stroke, pricking their fingers or ears with a needle to bleed will cure it.
scientific_fact: Pricking fingers or ears does not treat a stroke. A stroke is a brain emergency, and fast hospital treatment is what saves brain function.
possibilities: 1. Wasted Time: Every minute without treatment damages brain cells.\n2. Infection Risk: Needle pricking can cause infection.\n3. Recognition: Face drooping, arm weakness and speech trouble are warning signs.
safe_alternatives: 1. Call emergency services immediately if you see these signs.\n2. Note the time symptoms started.\n3. Do not give food, drink or home remedies.
verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), American Heart Association (AHA)

claim_keywords: carrots eyesight glasses remove
viral_myth: Eating lots of carrots removes the need for glasses.
scientific_fact: Vitamin A in carrots supports eye health, but carrots cannot correct refractive errors like short-sightedness.
possibilities: 1. Vitamin A: Deficiency harms eyes, but most people get enough.\n2. Refractive Error: It is due to eye shape, not diet.\n3. Risk: Skipping eye tests delays diagnosis.
safe_alternatives: 1. Get your eyes tested regularly.\n2. Wear prescribed glasses or lenses.\n3. Eat a varied diet with vegetables and fruit.
verified_sources: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: reading dim light phone screen damage eyes permanently
viral_myth: Reading in dim light or using phones damages your eyes permanently.
scientific_fact: These habits can cause temporary eye strain, dryness and headaches, but there is no evidence of permanent eye damage in adults.
possibilities: 1. Eye Strain: Tired eyes recover with rest.\n2. Blink Rate: Screens reduce blinking, causing dryness.\n3. Real Concern: Persistent symptoms need an eye check.
safe_alternatives: 1. Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.\n2. Use good lighting and take screen breaks.\n3. See an eye doctor for ongoing discomfort.
verified_sources: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: pregnant eating for two double food
viral_myth: Pregnant women must eat double the food because they are eating for two.
scientific_fact: Pregnancy needs only a small amount of extra energy, mostly in the last trimester. Food quality matters more than quantity.
possibilities: 1. Small Increase: Extra calories needed are modest.\n2. Quality: Iron, folate, protein and calcium are priorities.\n3. Risk: Overeating raises the risk of excess weight gain and diabetes.
safe_alternatives: 1. Eat a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables, pulses, milk and fruit.\n2. Take iron and folic acid as prescribed.\n3. Attend regular antenatal checkups.
verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: pregnancy exercise avoid walking safe
viral_myth: Pregnant women should avoid all exercise.
scientific_fact: For most uncomplicated pregnancies, regular moderate activity like walking is safe and recommended. Women should check with their doctor first.
possibilities: 1. Benefits: Exercise supports energy, mood and healthy weight gain.\n2. Exceptions: Some conditions require rest.\n3. Warning Signs: Bleeding, dizziness or pain need medical advice.
safe_alternatives: 1. Ask your doctor what activity is right for you.\n2. Choose walking, gentle yoga or swimming.\n3. Stop and seek care if you feel unwell.
verified_sources: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: newborn water gripe water honey before six months
viral_myth: Newborns need water, gripe water or honey in the first six months.
scientific_fact: Babies should be exclusively breastfed for the first six months with no water or other foods. Honey must not be given to babies under 12 months because of infant botulism.
possibilities: 1. Breast Milk: It provides all the fluid and nutrition a baby needs.\n2. Infection Risk: Water and other liquids can introduce germs.\n3. Honey Danger: It can cause a serious illness in infants.
safe_alternatives: 1. Breastfeed on demand for the first six months.\n2. Start complementary foods at six months as advised.\n3. Ask a health worker for breastfeeding support.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: depression weakness positive thinking enough
viral_myth: Depression is just weakness, and positive thinking is enough to overcome it.
scientific_fact: Depression is a medical condition that affects mood, sleep and energy. It is treatable with therapy, medicines and support.
possibilities: 1. Medical Condition: It is not a personal failing.\n2. Treatable: Many people recover with proper care.\n3. Risk: Dismissing it delays help.
safe_alternatives: 1. Talk to a doctor or mental health professional.\n2. Reach out to trusted family or friends.\n3. Use helplines if you feel hopeless or unsafe.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

claim_keywords: mental illness violent dangerous people
viral_myth: People with mental illness are dangerous and violent.
scientific_fact: Most people with mental illness are not violent. They are more likely to be victims of violence than to harm others.
possibilities: 1. Stigma: Fear leads to isolation and delayed treatment.\n2. Real Picture: Violence is rare among people with mental illness.\n3. Support: Treatment and community care help recovery.
safe_alternatives: 1. Treat people with mental illness with respect.\n2. Encourage them to seek professional care.\n3. Learn from reliable mental health sources.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

claim_keywords: cancer contagious catch touch
viral_myth: Cancer is contagious and can spread from person to person.
scientific_fact: Cancer cannot be caught from another person. Some infections like HPV and hepatitis B raise cancer risk, but cancer itself is not contagious.
possibilities: 1. Not Infectious: Cancer cells from one person do not take hold in another.\n2. Infection Link: Certain viruses can lead to cancer over time.\n3. Stigma Harm: The myth isolates patients.
safe_alternatives: 1. Support and spend time with people who have cancer.\n2. Get HPV and hepatitis B vaccines where recommended.\n3. Attend recommended cancer screenings.
verified_sources: National Cancer Institute (NCI), American Cancer Society (ACS)

claim_keywords: sugar feeds cancer cut sugar starve tumor cure
viral_myth: Cutting out all sugar starves cancer cells and cures cancer.
scientific_fact: All cells use glucose, and there is no evidence that a sugar-free diet cures cancer. A healthy diet helps overall but must not replace treatment.
possibilities: 1. Glucose Use: Healthy and cancer cells both use sugar.\n2. Extreme Diets: They can cause weakness and malnutrition.\n3. Real Link: Obesity raises the risk of some cancers.
safe_alternatives: 1. Follow the diet plan from your oncology team or dietitian.\n2. Limit sugary drinks and sweets as part of a healthy diet.\n3. Do not delay or replace cancer treatment.
verified_sources: National Cancer Institute (NCI), American Cancer Society (ACS)

claim_keywords: biopsy spreads cancer needle test
viral_myth: A biopsy spreads cancer, so you should avoid it.
scientific_fact: A biopsy does not spread cancer and is needed to diagnose it. The risk of spreading is extremely small.
possibilities: 1. Diagnosis Need: Treatment depends on knowing the exact type.\n2. Risk: Avoiding it delays diagnosis.\n3. Safety: Surgeons and radiologists use careful techniques.
safe_alternatives: 1. Discuss concerns with your doctor before the test.\n2. Get the biopsy done at a reputable center.\n3. Follow the treatment plan after diagnosis.

possibilities: 1. Skin damage: Long use thins skin.\n2. Dependence: Skin can flare when stopped.\n3. Hidden steroids: Some creams do not list them.
safe_alternatives: 1. Use skin creams only as prescribed.\n2. Read labels and avoid mixed 'fairness' creams.\n3. See a dermatologist for rashes or acne.
verified_sources: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD), Indian Association of Dermatologists, Venereologists and Leprologists (IADVL)

claim_keywords: tattoo piercing roadside infection hepatitis needle
viral_myth: Tattoos or piercings from roadside shops are safe if the needle looks clean.
scientific_fact: Unsterile needles can spread infections such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV, and cause skin infections. Only licensed shops using new, sterile needles are safe.
possibilities: 1. Unsterile tools: They can carry blood infections.\n2. Skin infection: Poor aftercare can infect the site.\n3. Hard to check: Clean-looking needles may not be sterile.
safe_alternatives: 1. Choose a licensed studio using single-use sterile needles.\n2. Follow aftercare instructions.\n3. See a doctor if the area is red, swollen or oozing.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: crash diet skip meals weight loss teenager
viral_myth: Crash dieting or skipping meals is a healthy way for teenagers to lose weight.
scientific_fact: Teenagers are still growing and need enough nutrients. Crash diets can cause tiredness, weakness, poor concentration and unhealthy eating patterns. Weight concerns should be discussed with a doctor or dietitian.
possibilities: 1. Growth needs: Teens need steady nutrition.\n2. Side effects: Fatigue and poor focus.\n3. Eating habits: Crash diets can lead to unhealthy patterns.
safe_alternatives: 1. Talk to a doctor or dietitian about weight concerns.\n2. Eat regular balanced meals and stay active.\n3. Avoid extreme diets suggested online.
verified_sources: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: weight loss powder pills fat burner social media
viral_myth: Weight-loss pills, powders or teas promoted on social media are safe for teenagers.
scientific_fact: Many such products are unregulated, and some contain hidden drugs that can harm the heart or liver. Teenagers should not use them.
possibilities: 1. Unregulated: Contents may be wrong or unsafe.\n2. Hidden drugs: Some contain stimulants.\n3. Marketing: Influencer claims lack evidence.
safe_alternatives: 1. Ask a doctor about healthy weight goals.\n2. Focus on balanced meals and activity.\n3. Avoid supplements promoted online.
verified_sources: US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: night eating raat khana fat weight
viral_myth: Eating at night automatically makes you fat.
scientific_fact: Weight depends on total energy eaten compared with energy used across the day. Heavy late meals can disturb sleep, but the clock itself is not the cause.
possibilities: 1. Total energy: This decides weight.\n2. Sleep: Heavy late meals can disturb it.\n3. Snacking: Late snacking can add extra calories.
safe_alternatives: 1. Eat dinner a couple of hours before sleep when possible.\n2. Choose lighter, balanced dinners.\n3. Avoid late-night junk snacking.
verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), Harvard Health Publishing

claim_keywords: rice roti carbs fat avoid carbohydrate
viral_myth: Rice and roti make you fat, so teenagers should avoid carbs.
scientific_fact: Carbohydrates are the body's main energy source and part of a balanced diet. Weight gain comes from eating more than you use, not from carbs alone.
possibilities: 1. Energy source: The body needs carbs.\n2. Portions: Quantity matters.\n3. Quality: Whole grains are better.
safe_alternatives: 1. Eat sensible portions of rice or roti with dal and vegetables.\n2. Choose whole grains when possible.\n3. Stay physically active.
verified_sources: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians, National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: cold drink soda daily exercise sugar aerated
viral_myth: Daily cold drinks are harmless if you exercise.
scientific_fact: Sugary drinks add a lot of sugar and calories and are linked to weight gain and tooth decay. They are best kept occasional.
possibilities: 1. Sugar load: One bottle has a lot of sugar.\n2. Dental harm: Sugar and acid affect teeth.\n3. Exercise: It does not cancel the effects.
safe_alternatives: 1. Drink water, nimbu pani without much sugar, or buttermilk.\n2. Keep soft drinks for rare occasions.\n3. Rinse your mouth with water afterward.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians

claim_keywords: packaged juice real fruit juice sugar fiber
viral_myth: Packaged fruit juice is as healthy as eating fruit.
scientific_fact: Packaged juices often contain added sugar and little fiber. Whole fruit is more filling and generally better.
possibilities: 1. Added sugar: Many packs contain it.\n2. Less fiber: Juicing removes fiber.\n3. Portion: Juice is easy to overdrink.
safe_alternatives: 1. Eat whole fruit instead of juice.\n2. Check the label for added sugar.\n3. Keep juice to small servings.
verified_sources: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians, National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: garam taseer eggs dry fruits mango pimples body heat
viral_myth: Eating 'garam' foods like eggs, dry fruits or mangoes causes pimples and body heat.
scientific_fact: There is no scientific basis for 'hot' or 'cold' foods causing pimples or body heat. Acne is linked to hormones and skin factors.
possibilities: 1. Traditional idea: It is not a medical concept.\n2. Acne causes: Hormones and oil.\n3. Diet effect: High-sugar diets may matter for some.
safe_alternatives: 1. Eat a balanced diet.\n2. Use acne care advised by a dermatologist.\n3. Do not avoid healthy foods without a reason.
verified_sources: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: curd banana night cold khasi raat
viral_myth: Eating curd or bananas at night causes cold and cough.
scientific_fact: Colds are caused by viruses, not by food eaten at night.
possibilities: 1. Virus cause: Colds spread through germs.\n2. No link: Curd and bananas do not cause infection.\n3. Coincidence: Illness may start by chance.
safe_alternatives: 1. Wash hands often to avoid colds.\n2. Eat balanced meals at regular times.\n3. Rest and drink fluids if you have a cold.
verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: thin skinny healthy weight patla
viral_myth: A thin teenager is always healthy.
scientific_fact: Being thin does not guarantee good nutrition. Teenagers can be underweight or have anemia and vitamin deficiencies. Health depends on diet, activity and medical checks.
possibilities: 1. Hidden deficiency: Thin people can lack nutrients.\n2. Underweight risks: Poor growth and low energy.\n3. Overall health: Diet and activity matter.
safe_alternatives: 1. Eat regular balanced meals.\n2. Get check-ups at school or clinic.\n3. See a doctor if weight is unusually low.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians

claim_keywords: iron folic acid tablets blue tablet WIFS anemia school
viral_myth: Teenagers who eat well don't need iron and folic acid tablets.
scientific_fact: Anemia is common among Indian adolescents. India's weekly iron and folic acid supplementation programme recommends tablets for adolescents, taken as advised by health workers.
possibilities: 1. Common problem: Anemia affects many teens.\n2. Program: Weekly tablets are offered in schools.\n3. Diet alone: It may not be enough.
safe_alternatives: 1. Take the weekly tablet as advised by health workers.\n2. Eat greens, pulses and vitamin C foods.\n3. Ask a doctor if you feel very tired or pale.
verified_sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: anemia jaggery dates beetroot khoon ki kami cure
viral_myth: Jaggery, dates or beetroot alone cure anemia.
scientific_fact: These foods contain some iron and help, but anemia needs proper testing and treatment, often with iron tablets, as advised by a doctor.
possibilities: 1. Some iron: These foods help a little.\n2. Testing needed: Anemia has different causes.\n3. Treatment: Tablets may be required.
safe_alternatives: 1. Get a hemoglobin test if you feel weak or pale.\n2. Take iron tablets as prescribed.\n3. Eat iron-rich foods with vitamin C.
verified_sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: exam skip meals focus study fasting
viral_myth: Skipping meals helps you stay alert while studying.
scientific_fact: The brain needs regular energy. Skipping meals can cause tiredness, headaches and poor concentration.
possibilities: 1. Low energy: Skipped meals reduce focus.\n2. Headaches: Hunger can cause them.\n3. Overeating: Skipping can lead to binge snacking.
safe_alternatives: 1. Eat regular meals and healthy snacks during exams.\n2. Drink enough water.\n3. Avoid relying on junk food.
verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)

claim_keywords: almonds brain tonic memory topper yaddasht
viral_myth: Soaked almonds or brain tonics guarantee better memory and marks.
scientific_fact: No food or tonic can reliably improve memory in healthy students. Sleep, regular meals, practice and revision matter most.

safe_alternatives: 1. Sleep well and revise regularly.\n2. Eat balanced meals.\n3. Do not spend money on memory tonics.
verified_sources: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: protein powder supplement gym teens need
viral_myth: Teenagers need protein powders to build muscle.
scientific_fact: Most teenagers can meet protein needs through food such as dal, milk, eggs and paneer. Supplements are not necessary and may be poorly regulated.
possibilities: 1. Food first: Meals provide enough protein.\n2. Quality risk: Some products are mislabeled.\n3. Cost: Supplements are expensive.
safe_alternatives: 1. Include dal, milk, curd, eggs or paneer in meals.\n2. Train properly and sleep well.\n3. Ask a doctor before using supplements.
verified_sources: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

claim_keywords: whey protein steroid kidney damage
viral_myth: Whey protein is a steroid that damages teenagers' bodies.
scientific_fact: Whey is a protein from milk and is not a steroid. The real risks are unnecessary use and contaminated or mislabeled products.

claim_keywords: creatine steroid teens gym

verified_sources: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), Mayo Clinic

claim_keywords: steroid injection gym body fast short course
viral_myth: Taking steroids for a short time is safe for building a body fast.

claim_keywords: crunches belly fat spot reduction pet

scientific_fact: You cannot burn fat from one body area by exercising only that area. Fat loss comes from overall energy balance and activity.

verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), Mayo Clinic

scientific_fact: Mild muscle soreness is normal, but sharp or lasting pain, swelling or joint pain can signal injury.

verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)

claim_keywords: girls weights bulky masculine strength training

possibilities: 1. Hormones: Girls have less testosterone.\n2. Benefits: Strength and bone health.\n3. Technique: Proper form matters.

verified_sources: Mayo Clinic, National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: sweat fat burn sweating weight
viral_myth: More sweating means more fat is burnt.
scientific_fact: Sweat is the body's cooling system, not fat burning. Weight lost by sweating is water and returns after drinking.
possibilities: 1. Cooling: Sweat cools the body.\n2. Water loss: It is not fat loss.\n3. Heat risk: Sweat suits can be dangerous.
safe_alternatives: 1. Drink water during exercise.\n2. Do not use sweat suits or saunas to lose weight.\n3. Focus on steady activity and balanced meals.
verified_sources: Mayo Clinic, National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: daily workout no rest day muscle recovery overtraining
viral_myth: Training the same muscles every day without rest builds muscle faster.
scientific_fact: Muscles grow during recovery. Rest days and sleep help prevent overuse injury.
possibilities: 1. Recovery: Growth happens during rest.\n2. Overuse: Too much training causes injury.\n3. Fatigue: It lowers performance.
safe_alternatives: 1. Plan rest days each week.\n2. Alternate muscle groups.\n3. Sleep well.
verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)

claim_keywords: girls sports fertility harm khel ladkiyan
viral_myth: Playing sports harms girls' health or fertility.
scientific_fact: Regular physical activity is healthy for girls. WHO recommends daily physical activity for children and adolescents.
possibilities: 1. Health benefits: Activity supports bones, heart and mood.\n2. Fertility: Sports do not harm it.\n3. Social myth: The belief limits girls.
safe_alternatives: 1. Encourage regular play and sports for girls.\n2. Wear suitable gear and eat well.\n3. Talk to a doctor about any specific concern.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: exercise exam time waste study padhai
viral_myth: Exercise wastes study time during exams.
scientific_fact: Physical activity improves focus, mood and sleep and can help with exam stress.
possibilities: 1. Better focus: Movement helps concentration.\n2. Stress relief: It lowers tension.\n3. Sleep: It improves rest.
safe_alternatives: 1. Take short walks or stretch between study sessions.\n2. Keep regular activity during exams.\n3. Sleep enough.
verified_sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: sleep teen hours 5 6 hours enough neend
viral_myth: Teenagers only need 5 to 6 hours of sleep; sleeping more is laziness.
scientific_fact: Teenagers generally need about 8 to 10 hours of sleep. Sleeping too little affects mood, memory, grades and health.
possibilities: 1. Biology: Teens need more sleep.\n2. Effects: Mood and memory suffer.\n3. Myth: Needing sleep is not laziness.
safe_alternatives: 1. Keep a regular bedtime and wake time.\n2. Avoid phones before sleep.\n3. Talk to a doctor if you cannot sleep.
verified_sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)

claim_keywords: all night study raat jagna exam topper
viral_myth: Studying all night before an exam is the best way to score well.
scientific_fact: Sleep helps the brain store what you learned. All-nighters reduce attention and recall.
possibilities: 1. Memory: Sleep consolidates learning.\n2. Attention: Tiredness lowers focus.\n3. Exam day: Poor sleep hurts performance.
safe_alternatives: 1. Study in planned sessions earlier.\n2. Sleep before the exam.\n3. Take short breaks while studying.
verified_sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: weekend sleep catch up late sleeping
viral_myth: Sleeping late on weekends fully makes up for lost sleep.
scientific_fact: Extra weekend sleep helps a little but does not fully undo regular short sleep. A steady schedule is better.
possibilities: 1. Partial recovery: It helps only a little.\n2. Irregular rhythm: It disturbs body clock.\n3. Weekday habits: These matter more.
safe_alternatives: 1. Keep a steady sleep schedule.\n2. Avoid very late nights during the week.\n3. Limit screens before bed.
verified_sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: coffee tea study night caffeine safe
viral_myth: Drinking lots of tea or coffee is a safe way to study through the night.
scientific_fact: Caffeine gives short-term alertness but can cause jitters, fast heartbeat, headaches and disturbed sleep.
possibilities: 1. Short boost: Alertness fades.\n2. Side effects: Jitters and palpitations.\n3. Sleep loss: It harms the next day.
safe_alternatives: 1. Limit caffeine and avoid it late.\n2. Drink water and take breaks.\n3. Sleep instead of staying up.
verified_sources: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: teen depression anxiety exam tension attention seeking
viral_myth: Teenage depression or anxiety is just exam stress or attention-seeking.
scientific_fact: Depression and anxiety are real conditions in teenagers and can be treated. Persistent sadness, loss of interest or changes in sleep or appetite need support from a doctor or counselor.
possibilities: 1. Real condition: These are not attention-seeking.\n2. Signs: Persistent sadness, withdrawal or sleep change.\n3. Treatable: Support helps.
safe_alternatives: 1. Talk to a trusted adult, doctor or counselor.\n2. Do not dismiss a friend's distress.\n3. Use helplines such as Tele-MANAS (14416) if needed.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

claim_keywords: ask suicide thoughts idea head talk teenager
viral_myth: Asking a teenager about suicidal thoughts puts the idea in their head.
scientific_fact: Asking caringly does not cause suicidal thoughts and can help a person open up and get support. If someone is in danger, get help immediately.
possibilities: 1. Open talk: It can reduce isolation.\n2. Safety: Asking is part of prevention.\n3. Help: Professionals can support.
safe_alternatives: 1. Listen without judgment and stay with the person.\n2. Call emergency services (112) if there is immediate danger.\n3. Use Tele-MANAS (14416) or a school counselor.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

claim_keywords: mental health hide shame log kya kahenge stigma
viral_myth: Mental health problems should be kept secret because they bring shame to the family.
scientific_fact: Mental health conditions are common and treatable. Hiding them delays help and can make them worse.
possibilities: 1. Common: Many people experience them.\n2. Stigma: It stops people from seeking help.\n3. Treatment: Early help works best.
safe_alternatives: 1. Talk to a trusted adult or counselor.\n2. Learn from reliable mental health sources.\n3. Support friends who share their struggles.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

claim_keywords: counsellor psychologist pagal mad therapy
viral_myth: Only 'mad' people (pagal) go to a counselor or psychologist.
scientific_fact: Counselors and psychologists help with stress, anxiety, low mood and many everyday problems. Seeking help is a sign of strength.

safe_alternatives: 1. Ask a school counselor or doctor for guidance.\n2. Try Tele-MANAS (14416) for free support.\n3. Encourage friends to seek help early.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

claim_keywords: gaming mobile addiction habit pubg free fire
viral_myth: Excessive gaming or phone use is just a bad habit, never a health issue.
scientific_fact: WHO recognizes gaming disorder as a health condition when gaming harms sleep, studies, relationships or health. Most gamers are not affected, but warning signs deserve attention.
possibilities: 1. Warning signs: Lost control and neglected duties.\n2. Most gamers: Not everyone is affected.\n3. Support: Counseling can help.
safe_alternatives: 1. Set time limits and take breaks.\n2. Keep sleep and study routines.\n3. Talk to a counselor if gaming is harming daily life.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: yoga breathing pranayama exam stress anxiety
viral_myth: Yoga and breathing exercises cannot help with exam stress.
scientific_fact: Studies suggest yoga, slow breathing and mindfulness can help reduce stress for many people, though they do not replace treatment for serious conditions.
possibilities: 1. Calming effect: Slow breathing relaxes the body.\n2. Not a cure: Serious conditions need treatment.\n3. Routine: Regular practice helps.
safe_alternatives: 1. Practice slow breathing for a few minutes daily.\n2. Combine it with sleep and exercise.\n3. Seek help if stress is overwhelming.
verified_sources: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: study drugs modafinil ritalin focus tablets exam
viral_myth: Tablets sold to boost focus for exams are safe to take without a prescription.
scientific_fact: Stimulants and similar prescription medicines can cause serious side effects including heart problems, anxiety and addiction when used without medical supervision.

safe_alternatives: 1. Use sleep, breaks and a study plan instead.\n2. Talk to a doctor about concentration problems.\n3. Never use medicines meant for others.
verified_sources: National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)

claim_keywords: e-cigarette vape india legal safer
viral_myth: E-cigarettes and vapes are legal, safe alternatives to smoking for teenagers in India.
scientific_fact: Vapes contain nicotine and harmful chemicals. In India, the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019 bans their manufacture, sale and import.
possibilities: 1. Nicotine: Vapes are addictive.\n2. Chemicals: Aerosols contain harmful substances.\n3. Law: Sale is banned in India.
safe_alternatives: 1. Do not start vaping.\n2. Use Tele-MANAS or a doctor for quitting support.\n3. Talk to a counselor if you feel pressure.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

claim_keywords: occasional smoking party harmless social smoking
viral_myth: Smoking only occasionally at parties does no harm.
scientific_fact: No level of tobacco use is safe, and nicotine can cause dependence quickly in teenagers.
possibilities: 1. No safe level: Every cigarette adds risk.\n2. Dependence: It can start fast.\n3. Peer pressure: It is common at parties.
safe_alternatives: 1. Practice saying no with a ready line.\n2. Choose friends who respect your choice.\n3. Seek quit support early.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: smoking reduce stress tension relief
viral_myth: Smoking reduces stress.

possibilities: 1. Withdrawal relief: It is temporary.\n2. More stress: Dependence raises anxiety.\n3. Health: It harms the lungs and heart.
safe_alternatives: 1. Try exercise, walks or breathing for stress.\n2. Talk to a counselor.\n3. Get help quitting.
verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: energy drink red bull monster teens safe

safe_alternatives: 1. Drink water, milk or nimbu pani.\n2. Sleep enough for natural energy.\n3. Avoid mixing with exercise or alcohol.
verified_sources: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: beer wine light alcohol harmless teens

verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

claim_keywords: alcohol sleep relax neend drink

verified_sources: National Health Service (NHS), National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA)

claim_keywords: ganja bhang weed natural harmless cannabis

scientific_fact: Cannabis can affect memory, attention, mood and mental health, especially in teenagers, and can cause dependence.

claim_keywords: cough syrup sleeping pills nasha medicine safe high
viral_myth: Using cough syrup or sleeping pills to get high is safe because they're medicines.
scientific_fact: Misusing medicines can cause overdose, breathing problems, addiction and death.

verified_sources: National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: addicted try once weekend only nasha

claim_keywords: passive smoke friends cigarette dhuan secondhand

claim_keywords: kissing pregnancy ho jata hai

claim_keywords: first time pregnancy cannot girl

claim_keywords: emergency contraceptive pill i-pill abortion harmful
viral_myth: The emergency contraceptive pill is an abortion pill and is harmful.
scientific_fact: Emergency contraception works mainly by delaying ovulation, does not end an existing pregnancy, and is not meant for regular use. It works better the sooner it is taken. A doctor or pharmacist can advise.
possibilities: 1. Not abortion: It does not end a pregnancy.\n2. Timing: Sooner is better.\n3. Not regular: It is for emergencies.
safe_alternatives: 1. Ask a doctor or pharmacist for advice.\n2. Use regular contraception for ongoing protection.\n3. See a doctor if periods are delayed afterward.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: condom fail holes infection work
viral_myth: Condoms don't work or cause infections.
scientific_fact: Used correctly every time, condoms greatly reduce the risk of pregnancy and many infections including HIV.
possibilities: 1. Effective: Correct use matters.\n2. STI protection: They reduce risk.\n3. Misuse: Errors cause failures.
safe_alternatives: 1. Learn correct use from a health worker.\n2. Check expiry dates.\n3. Ask a doctor about other protection.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

scientific_fact: HIV spreads through blood, unprotected sex and from mother to child. It does not spread through casual contact, mosquitoes or sharing food.
possibilities: 1. Real routes: Blood, sex and mother to child.\n2. Casual contact: It is safe.\n3. Stigma: The myth harms people.

verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO)

claim_keywords: hiv death sentence aids cure
viral_myth: HIV means certain early death.
scientific_fact: With antiretroviral treatment (ART), people with HIV can live long, healthy lives. ART is available free through government centers under NACO.
possibilities: 1. Treatment: ART controls the virus.\n2. Early care: Early treatment works best.\n3. Stigma: Fear delays testing.
safe_alternatives: 1. Get tested if you may have been exposed.\n2. Start ART early as advised.\n3. Seek support from counselors.
verified_sources: World Health Organization (WHO), National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO)

viral_myth: Only 'bad' people get STIs, and you can tell by looking at someone.
scientific_fact: Anyone who is sexually active can get an STI, and many infections show no symptoms.
possibilities: 1. No stereotype: Anyone can be affected.\n2. Silent infections: Symptoms may be absent.\n3. Testing: It is the only way to know.

viral_myth: A medical 'virginity test' can show whether a girl has had sex.
scientific_fact: There is no scientific basis for virginity tests. WHO says they have no scientific validity and are harmful.

possibilities: 1. Evidence: Education supports safer choices.\n2. Silence: It leaves room for rumors.\n3. Age-appropriate: Content should suit age.

claim_keywords: hpv vaccine sexually active girls cervical
viral_myth: The HPV vaccine encourages girls to become sexually active.
scientific_fact: Studies show HPV vaccination does not lead to earlier or increased sexual activity, and it protects against cervical cancer.

verified_sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: spectacles chashma eyes weak power increase glasses
viral_myth: Wearing glasses makes your eyesight weaker.
scientific_fact: Glasses correct blurred vision and do not worsen the eyes. Power may change as teenagers grow, which is why regular checks matter.
possibilities: 1. Correction: Glasses help you see clearly.\n2. Natural change: Power can change with growth.\n3. Not wearing: It can cause headaches and strain.
safe_alternatives: 1. Get an eye test if you have blurred vision or headaches.\n2. Wear glasses as advised.\n3. Have yearly eye checks.
verified_sources: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO), National Health Service (NHS)

claim_keywords: kajal surma eyes children vision lead
viral_myth: Applying kajal or surma inside the eyes improves vision.
scientific_fact: Some traditional kajal or surma products contain lead and can cause infection or eye irritation. They do not improve eyesight.

safe_alternatives: 1. Avoid putting kajal inside the eyes.\n2. Use tested cosmetics only outside the eye.\n3. See an eye doctor for eye problems.

viral_myth: Brushing harder cleans teeth better.
scientific_fact: Hard brushing can damage gums and enamel. Gentle brushing twice a day with a soft brush is better.
possibilities: 1. Gum damage: Hard brushing wears gums.\n2. Enamel wear: It harms teeth.\n3. Technique: Gentle brushing works.
safe_alternatives: 1. Brush twice daily with a soft brush.\n2. Use fluoride toothpaste.\n3. Visit a dentist regularly.

viral_myth: Datun, charcoal powder or salt are better than fluoride toothpaste.
scientific_fact: Fluoride toothpaste reduces cavities. Charcoal or salt can be abrasive and are not proven to be better.
possibilities: 1. Fluoride: It protects teeth.\n2. Abrasive: Charcoal can wear enamel.\n3. Tradition: It is not always better.
safe_alternatives: 1. Use fluoride toothpaste twice a day.\n2. Limit sugary snacks.\n3. See a dentist for problems.
verified_sources: American Dental Association (ADA), World Health Organization (WHO)

claim_keywords: viruddha ahar incompatible food combinations poison milk sour

scientific_fact: There is no scientific evidence that common food combinations cause poisoning or skin disease. Spoiled or unsafe food is the real risk.

scientific_fact: Heavy backpacks can cause back, shoulder and posture problems. Experts advise keeping the load light, and India's Ministry of Education issued a school bag policy to limit weight.
possibilities: 1. Posture: Heavy loads strain the back.\n2. Pain: Shoulder and back pain can follow.\n3. Policy: Guidelines exist.
safe_alternatives: 1. Carry only what is needed.\n2. Use both straps and pack heavy items close to the back.\n3. Tell a teacher or parent if you have pain.
verified_sources: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), Ministry of Education (India)

scientific_fact: Over-the-counter painkillers should be taken only as the label or a doctor advises. Overuse can cause stomach problems, kidney or liver harm and rebound headaches.
